stem: A client with vomiting and poor intake is clinically volume depleted and has an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The elevation can support a prerenal process related to water depletion or reduced renal perfusion when interpreted with the clinical picture and other renal data.
options.B: The elevation specifically proves postrenal urinary obstruction regardless of the client's volume status or other findings.
options.C: The elevation demonstrates improved glomerular filtration because BUN rises as renal clearance becomes more efficient.
options.D: The elevation is unrelated to hydration or renal perfusion and should not influence assessment of a volume-depleted client.

rationale: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories information states that increased BUN can result from prerenal causes such as water depletion from decreased intake or excessive loss and cardiac decompensation/reduced renal perfusion, but BUN can also increase from renal and postrenal causes. It is therefore interpreted with the clinical picture and commonly alongside creatinine rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis. In this volume-depleted client, A is the appropriate interpretation. B overstates specificity for obstruction, C reverses the relationship to clearance, and D incorrectly dismisses the relevance of hydration and perfusion.
educational_objective: Interpret elevated BUN as a nonspecific finding that can support prerenal azotemia in a volume-depleted client when integrated with clinical status and other renal data rather than treating it as diagnostic by itself.
source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories Test Catalog live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Clinical Information: increased BUN may be due to prerenal causes including cardiac decompensation and water depletion from decreased intake/excessive loss; renal and postrenal causes are also listed. BUN is frequently requested with serum creatinine to aid differential diagnosis of prerenal, renal, and postrenal hyperuremia.
source_claim_supported: Elevated BUN in a clinically volume-depleted client can support a prerenal process from water depletion or reduced perfusion, but BUN is nonspecific and requires contextual interpretation.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret laboratory findings and trends, recognize risk related to fluid volume/perfusion changes, and integrate diagnostic data with client condition.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — BUN interpretation in volume depletion

options.A: The elevation can support a prerenal process related to water depletion or reduced renal perfusion when interpreted with the clinical picture.
options.B: The elevation specifically proves postrenal urinary obstruction regardless of the client's volume status or other findings.

source_original.rationale: BUN can increase in prerenal states such as water depletion and reduced renal perfusion. Option A appropriately interprets the result in the clinical context without treating BUN as diagnostic by itself. B overstates specificity, C reverses the meaning, and D is false.
source_original.source_detail: Clinical Information/Interpretation: BUN may rise in prerenal states including water depletion and reduced renal perfusion/cardiac decompensation; BUN and creatinine are interpreted together with the clinical picture and other data. Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories BUN test catalog entry 81793; live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic/laboratory interpretation, postprocedure monitoring, device management and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the stem and key A. Tightened A to explicitly preserve BUN's nonspecific nature and its interpretation with other renal data, matching the current Mayo catalog and preventing a prerenal finding from being presented as a stand-alone diagnosis.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog; official NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: Mayo BUN Clinical Information and paired BUN/creatinine interpretation statement
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item states only that elevated BUN can support a prerenal process in the given clinical context and explicitly avoids claiming diagnostic specificity.

distractor_audit.A: Correct; fits volume depletion while preserving nonspecificity.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because BUN alone does not prove postrenal obstruction.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because BUN does not rise as a marker of improved clearance.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because water depletion/reduced perfusion are recognized causes of increased BUN.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A appropriately integrates the result with the stated volume-depleted clinical picture without overclaiming causality.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are interpretations of the same BUN result and are parallel in scope.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential — renal laboratory and volume-status interpretation.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current Mayo clinical information, each alternative, rationale, objective, NCSBN mapping, ambiguity and cueing. A remained uniquely correct.
